The text studies criteria for determining when certain morphic sequences are almost periodic, in the sense of being uniformly recurrent. In other words, it is concerned with identifying when every finite factor that appears in a sequence reappears throughout the sequence with bounded gaps.

A central case considered is that of fixed points of non-erasing morphisms. These are infinite sequences generated by repeatedly applying a morphism that never maps a letter to the empty word. For this class of morphic sequences, the text establishes effective criteria for deciding almost periodicity.

The discussion also treats automatic sequences as another important class. Since automatic sequences form a well-studied subclass of morphic sequences with strong computational structure, they provide a natural setting in which to investigate decidability questions related to uniform recurrence.

In both of these cases—fixed points of non-erasing morphisms and automatic sequences—the text provides a polynomial-time algorithm for deciding whether the sequence is almost periodic. This gives not only a theoretical characterization but also an efficient computational method for solving the problem in these settings.

Overall, the results presented support the broader conjecture that the general problem of deciding almost periodicity for morphic sequences is decidable. By proving decidability, and even polynomial-time decidability, in significant special cases, the text offers evidence that a complete solution to the general problem may be attainable.
outputs.L4:
The text studies the problem of deciding when morphic sequences are almost periodic, also known as uniformly recurrent. A morphic sequence is an infinite sequence generated from a morphism, possibly followed by a coding, and such sequences form an important class in combinatorics on words and theoretical computer science. Almost periodicity means that every finite factor that appears in the sequence reappears infinitely often with bounded gaps. In other words, no factor disappears for arbitrarily long stretches of the sequence.

The main focus is on two important cases in which the decidability problem can be treated effectively. First, the text considers fixed points of non-erasing morphisms, that is, morphisms that never map a letter to the empty word. For this class, it gives criteria that allow one to determine whether the resulting infinite word is almost periodic. These criteria can be checked algorithmically, and the corresponding decision procedure runs in polynomial time.

Second, the text examines automatic sequences, which are sequences generated by finite automata and which can also be viewed as a special class of morphic sequences. In this setting as well, the text shows that almost periodicity can be decided efficiently. The existence of polynomial-time algorithms for automatic sequences demonstrates that the property of uniform recurrence is not only theoretically decidable in these cases but also computationally tractable.

Overall, the results show that for significant subclasses of morphic sequences, the question of almost periodicity can be answered effectively and efficiently. These findings provide positive evidence for the broader conjecture that the general problem of deciding almost periodicity for arbitrary morphic sequences may also be decidable. While the full general case remains more challenging, the methods developed for non-erasing morphic fixed points and automatic sequences suggest that a complete decision procedure may be possible.

**Namely**

The word **“namely”** is used to introduce specific details, examples, or explanations about something that has just been mentioned. It helps make a statement clearer by identifying exactly what the speaker or writer means.

For example, someone might say, “There are two subjects I enjoy most, namely history and literature.” In this sentence, **“namely”** shows which two subjects are being discussed. It is often used in formal writing, essays, reports, and explanations because it adds precision and clarity.

“Namely” is similar in meaning to phrases like **“that is,” “specifically,”** or **“in other words.”** However, it usually introduces a more exact definition or a complete list of items. For instance: “The company focuses on three main goals, namely innovation, customer satisfaction, and sustainability.”

Using **“namely”** correctly can make writing more organized and professional. It signals to the reader that important details are about to follow. Therefore, it is a useful word for explaining ideas clearly and directly.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract for a paper about criteria and algorithms for deciding almost periodicity (uniform recurrence) in morphic and automatic sequences.
counterfactuals.output: We study decision problems for almost periodicity (uniform recurrence) in morphic and automatic sequences. We establish effective criteria characterizing when a morphic sequence generated by a morphism and coding is uniformly recurrent, reducing the question to structural properties of the underlying substitution dynamics. For automatic sequences, we derive specialized finite-state conditions yielding efficient decision procedures. The resulting algorithms decide almost periodicity, identify relevant recurrent components, and apply uniformly across common representations of morphic and automatic words. These results provide a constructive bridge between symbolic dynamics, formal language theory, and automata-based methods for infinite sequences.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main results of a research article on morphic sequences, fixed points of non-erasing morphisms, and automatic sequences.
counterfactuals.output:
The article’s main results can be summarized as follows:

- **Morphic sequences can be generated without erasing morphisms.**  
  A central theorem shows that if an infinite sequence is morphic — i.e. obtained by applying a coding or morphism to a fixed point of a morphism — then it can also be represented using a **non-erasing morphism**. In other words, erasing letters are not essential for generating morphic sequences.

- **Fixed points of non-erasing morphisms are sufficiently general.**  
  The paper proves that the study of morphic sequences may be reduced to the study of fixed points of morphisms that never delete symbols. This gives a cleaner structural framework, because non-erasing morphisms behave better with respect to growth, iteration, and infinite fixed points.

- **The class of morphic sequences is stable under codings.**  
  Applying a letter-to-letter projection, or coding, to a fixed point of a non-erasing morphism still yields a morphic sequence. Conversely, every morphic sequence can be obtained in this way.

- **Connections with automatic sequences are clarified.**  
  Automatic sequences appear as a special subclass of morphic sequences. In particular, a sequence is **automatic** when it can be produced from the fixed point of a **uniform morphism**, meaning each letter is mapped to a word of the same length.

- **Uniform morphisms characterize automaticity.**  
  The article emphasizes the classical correspondence:  
  \[
  k\text{-automatic sequences}
  \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad
  \text{codings of fixed points of } k\text{-uniform morphisms}.
  \]
  Thus automatic sequences are precisely the morphic sequences arising from constant-length substitutions.

- **Erasing morphisms can be eliminated effectively.**  
  The paper gives constructive methods for replacing a morphic representation involving erasures by an equivalent representation using only non-erasing morphisms. This is important for algorithmic and structural applications.

- **Growth behavior plays a key role.**  
  The article analyzes how iterates of morphisms grow and uses this to distinguish general morphic sequences from automatic ones. Uniform growth corresponds to automaticity, while more general growth gives the broader class of morphic sequences.

Overall, the main contribution is to show that **non-erasing morphisms are sufficient to describe all morphic sequences**, and to situate **automatic sequences** as the constant-length, or uniform, case within the broader theory of morphic sequences.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a short mathematical abstract mentioning polynomial-time algorithms for determining whether certain morphic sequences are uniformly recurrent.
counterfactuals.output: We study decision problems for uniform recurrence in morphic sequences generated by iterated morphisms followed by codings. For broad classes of morphisms, including non-erasing substitutions with effectively computable growth structure, we establish polynomial-time algorithms to determine whether the associated infinite word is uniformly recurrent. The approach combines graph-theoretic analysis of the dependency digraph of letters with effective bounds on return-word behavior and periodic components. These results give a tractable criterion for uniform recurrence in several natural families of morphic sequences and clarify the boundary between decidable structural regularity and computational complexity in symbolic dynamics.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a brief conference-style description of results supporting decidability of almost periodicity for morphic sequences.
counterfactuals.output:
We present decidability results for almost periodicity of morphic sequences. A morphic sequence is obtained by iterating a morphism on a finite alphabet and then applying a coding; such sequences form a broad class including automatic and substitutive sequences. We show that, given a morphic presentation, it is decidable whether the resulting infinite word is almost periodic, equivalently uniformly recurrent: every finite factor that occurs appears with bounded gaps.

The proof combines structural properties of morphism growth with an effective analysis of the associated factor language. After reducing to a suitable normalized morphic representation, one can compute the relevant growth classes and determine which letters and factors persist in the limit word. The main criterion identifies whether all recurring factors have uniformly bounded return times; failure of almost periodicity is witnessed effectively by a factor whose gaps grow unboundedly. Thus the decision procedure not only answers yes or no, but can in principle produce a finite obstruction in the negative case.

These results extend classical decidability phenomena for automatic sequences to the wider morphic setting and clarify the algorithmic boundary between recurrence and uniform recurrence in morphic dynamics. They provide an effective tool for analyzing symbolic dynamical systems generated by substitutions and codings, with applications to combinatorics on words, automata theory, and the study of substitutive subshifts.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
